{{Short description|Parameter estimation technique in statistics}}{{For|the technique used to prove [[convergence in distribution]]|Method of moments (probability theory)}}In [[statistics]], the '''method of moments''' is a method of [[estimation]] of population [[statistical parameter|parameters]]. The same principle is used to derive higher moments like skewness and [[kurtosis]].

It starts by expressing the population [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] (i.e., the [[expected value]]s of powers of the [[random variable]] under consideration) as functions of the parameters of interest. Those expressions are then set equal to the sample moments. The number of such equations is the same as the number of parameters to be estimated. Those equations are then solved for the parameters of interest.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dodge |first=Yadolah |title=The Concise Encyclopedia of Statistics |date=2008 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |isbn=978-0-387-32833-1 |pages=348-349}}</ref> The solutions are estimates of those parameters. The method of moments was first introduced by [[Karl Pearson]] in 1895.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pearson |first=Karl |date=1895 |title=Contributions to the Mathematical Theory of Evolution. II. Skew Variation in Homogeneous Material |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/90649 |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A |volume=186 |pages=343-414}}</ref><ref name=":3" />  

==Method==
Suppose that the parameter <math>\theta</math> = (<math>\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots, \theta_k</math>) characterizes the [[probability distribution|distribution]] <math>f_W(w; \theta)</math> of the random variable <math>W</math>.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |year=1998 |title=Estimator: Method of Moments |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopedia of Statistical Sciences]] |publisher=Wiley |last=Bowman |first=Kimiko O. |author-link=Kimiko O. Bowman |pages=2092–2098 |last2=L. R. |first2=Shenton}}</ref> Suppose the first <math>k</math> moments of the true distribution (the "population moments") can be expressed as functions of the  <math>\theta</math>s:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
m_1 & \equiv \operatorname E[W]   = g_1(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_k) , \\[4pt]
m_2 & \equiv \operatorname E[W^2] = g_2(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_k), \\
& \,\,\, \vdots \\
m_k & \equiv \operatorname E[W^k] = g_k(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_k).
\end{align}
</math>

Suppose a sample of size <math>n</math> is drawn, resulting in the values <math>w_1, \dots, w_n</math>. For <math>j=1,\dots,k</math>, let 
<math display="block">\hat m_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^j</math> 
be the ''j''-th sample moment, an estimate of <math>m_j</math>. The method of moments estimator for <math>\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_k</math>  denoted by <math>\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2, \dots, \hat\theta_k </math> is defined to be a solution (if one exists) to the equations:<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Pearson |first=Karl |author-link=Karl Pearson |date=June 1936 |title=Method of Moments and Method of Maximum Likelihood |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2334123?origin=crossref |journal=Biometrika |volume=28 |issue=1/2 |pages=34 |doi=10.2307/2334123|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat m_1 & = g_1(\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2, \ldots, \hat\theta_k), \\[4pt]
\hat m_2 & = g_2(\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2, \ldots, \hat\theta_k), \\
& \,\,\, \vdots \\
\hat m_k & = g_k(\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2, \ldots, \hat\theta_k).
\end{align}</math>

The method described here for single random variables generalizes in an obvious manner to multiple random variables leading to multiple choices for moments to be used. Different choices generally lead to different solutions.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Quandt |first=Richard E. |author-link=Richard E. Quandt |last2=Ramsey |first2=James B. |author-link2=James B. Ramsey |date=December 1978 |title=Estimating Mixtures of Normal Distributions and Switching Regressions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2286266?origin=crossref |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |volume=73 |issue=364 |pages=730 |doi=10.2307/2286266}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Lindsay |first=Bruce G. |author-link=Bruce G. Lindsay |last2=Basak |first2=Prasanta |date=June 1993 |title=Multivariate Normal Mixtures: A Fast Consistent Method of Moments |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2290326?origin=crossref |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |volume=88 |issue=422 |pages=468 |doi=10.2307/2290326}}</ref>

== Properties ==
If it exists, a moment estimator <math>\hat{\theta}^{(n)}=(\hat\theta_1,\dots,\hat\theta_k)</math> based on an independent sample of <math>n</math> observations drawn from the distribution <math>f_W(w; \theta)</math> has the following statistical properties.

=== Consistency ===
Provided that the function <math>g=(g_1,\dots,g_k)</math> is [[Inverse function|invertible]] and [[Continuous function|continuous]], and the first <math>k</math> moments exist (<math>\operatorname E[|W|^k]<\infty</math>), the moment estimator is [[consistent estimator|strongly consistent]]. This is a direct consequence of the [[Law of large numbers|strong law of large numbers]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Shao |first=Jun |title=Mathematical Statistics |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-387-95382-3 |edition=2nd |pages=207}}</ref>

In the typical case, where the second moment <math>\mathbb E[\big(\hat\theta^{(n)}\big)^2]=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta^{(n)})+\mathbb E[\hat\theta^{(n)}]^2</math> does not explode as <math>n</math> goes to infinity, the above implies (by the [[Vitali convergence theorem]]) that the moment estimator is also [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)#Unbiasedness in the limit|unbiased in the limit]], that is,

<math display="block">\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[\hat\theta^{(n)}]=\theta.</math>

=== Asymptotic normality ===
If the function <math>g=(g_1,\dots,g_k)</math> is even [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] and <math>\operatorname E[|W^2|^k]<\infty</math>, then the moment estimator is also [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)#Asymptotic distribution|asymptotically normal]] in the sense<ref name=":5" /><math display="block">\sqrt{n}\big(\hat{\theta}^{(n)}-\mathbb{E}_\theta[\hat\theta^{(n)}]\big)\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ \mathcal N\big(0,(\nabla g^{-1}(\theta))^T\mathrm{Cov}_\theta(W)\nabla g^{-1}(\theta)\big),</math>where <math>\mathrm{Cov}_\theta(W)</math> is the [[covariance matrix]] of <math>W</math>. This is a consequence of the [[central limit theorem]] and the [[delta method]].

==Advantages and disadvantages==
On the one hand, the method of moments is fairly simple and broadly applicable, since it does not require any assumptions on the data distribution besides existence of the first few moments. This is particularly useful in settings, where the general shape of the distribution may not be known (e.g. [[utility|utility functions]]). Moreover, the resulting estimators are almost always consistent and [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)|asymptotically unbiased]].<ref name=":5" />

On the other hand, the moment equations do not always have a solution, in which case the method does not provide any estimator. In other cases, there might exist multiple solutions. In view of parameter estimation in a [[parametric model]], moment estimators are, in general, not [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)#asymptotic efficiency|asymptotically efficient]], in contrast to [[maximum likelihood estimators]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dodge |first=Yadolah |title=The Concise Encyclopedia of Statistics |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-387-32833-1 |pages=349}}</ref> Moreover, the method does not necessarily lead to [[sufficiency (statistics)|sufficient estimators]], i.e., they sometimes fail to take into account all relevant information in the sample.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Shao |first=Jun |title=Mathematical Statistics |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-387-95382-3 |edition=2nd |pages=208}}</ref>

== Alternative method of moments ==
{{More citations needed section|date=July 2026}}
The equations to be solved in the method of moments (MoM) are in general nonlinear and there are no generally applicable guarantees that tractable solutions exist{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}. But there is an alternative approach to using sample moments to estimate data model parameters in terms of known dependence of model moments on these parameters, and this alternative requires the solution of only linear equations or, more generally, tensor equations. This alternative is referred to as the [[Bayesian]]-Like MoM (BL-MoM), and it differs from the classical MoM in that it uses optimally weighted sample moments. Considering that the MoM is typically motivated by a lack of sufficient knowledge about the data model to determine likelihood functions and associated ''a posteriori'' probabilities of unknown or random parameters, it is odd that there exists a type of MoM that is ''Bayesian-Like''. But the particular meaning of ''Bayesian-Like'' leads to a problem formulation in which required knowledge of ''a posteriori'' probabilities is replaced with required knowledge of only the dependence of model moments on unknown model parameters, which is exactly the knowledge required by the traditional MoM.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hansen |first=Lars Peter |author-link=Lars Peter Hansen |date=July 1982 |title=Large Sample Properties of Generalized Method of Moments Estimators |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912775?origin=crossref |journal=Econometrica |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=1029 |doi=10.2307/1912775|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Lindsay1982">{{Cite journal |last=Lindsay |first=Bruce |author-link=Bruce G. Lindsay |date=December 1982 |title=Conditional Score Functions: Some Optimality Results |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2335985?origin=crossref |journal=Biometrika |volume=69 |issue=3 |pages=503 |doi=10.2307/2335985}}</ref> The BL-MoM also uses knowledge of ''a priori'' probabilities of the parameters to be estimated, when available, but otherwise uses uniform priors.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

The BL-MoM has been reported on in only the applied statistics literature in connection with parameter estimation and [[Statistical hypothesis test|hypothesis testing]] using observations of stochastic processes for problems in Information and Communications Theory and, in particular, communications receiver design in the absence of knowledge of likelihood functions or associated ''a posteriori'' probabilities<ref name="Gardner1981">{{Cite journal |last=Gardner |first=William |author-link=William A Gardner |date=May 1981 |title=Design of nearest prototype signal classifiers (Corresp.) |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1056334/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=368–372 |doi=10.1109/TIT.1981.1056334 |issn=0018-9448|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and references therein. In addition, the restatement of this receiver design approach for [[stochastic process]] models as an alternative to the classical MoM for any type of multivariate data is available in tutorial form at the university website.<ref name="cyclostationarity">[https://cyclostationarity.com Cyclostationarity], page 11.4</ref> The applications in<ref name="Gardner1981"/> and references demonstrate some important characteristics of this alternative to the classical MoM, and a detailed list of relative advantages and disadvantages is given in,<ref name="cyclostationarity"/> but the literature is missing direct comparisons in specific applications of the classical MoM and the BL-MoM.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

==Examples==
=== Poisson distribution ===
Let <math>W\sim \mathrm{Poiss}(\lambda)</math> be [[Poisson distribution|Poisson distributed]] with parameter <math>\lambda>0</math>. The first moment (that is, the mean) is

<math display="block">m_1=\operatorname E[W]=\lambda.</math>

Since this is already an explicit equation for <math>\lambda</math>, the moment estimator is simply the [[Sample mean and covariance|sample mean]].

=== Normal distribution ===
Let <math>W\sim \mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)</math> be [[Normal distribution|normally distributed]] with unknown parameters <math>\mu\in\R</math> and <math>\sigma^2>0</math>. Since two parameters must be determined, two equations are needed. The first two moments are given by

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&m_1 = \operatorname{E}[W] = \mu, \\
&m_2 = \operatorname{E}[W^2] = \mathrm{Var}(W) + \operatorname{E}[W]^2= \sigma^2+\mu^2.
\end{align}</math>

Solving the equations for the parameters yields

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mu &= m_1, \\
\sigma^2 &= m_2-m_1^2.
\end{align}</math>

Given a sample <math>X_1,\dots,X_n\sim \mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)</math>, the corresponding estimators are

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat\mu &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \overline X, \\
\hat\sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(X_i-\overline{X}\big)^2,
\end{align}</math>

which are the [[Sample mean and covariance|sample mean]] and the (biased) [[Variance|sample variance]]. In this case, they coincide with the [[Maximum likelihood estimation|maximum likelihood estimators]].

=== Uniform distribution ===
Consider the [[Uniform distribution (continuous)|uniform distribution]] on the interval <math>[a,b]</math>, <math>U(a,b)</math>, with unknown parameters <math>-\infty<a<b<\infty</math>. If <math>W\sim U(a,b)</math> then we have<ref name=":2" />

<math display="block">\begin{align}
m_1 &= \operatorname E\left[W\right]   &=& \tfrac{1}{2}(a + b) \\[1ex]
m_2 &= \operatorname E\left[W^2\right] &=& \tfrac{1}{3} \left(a^2 + ab + b^2\right)
\end{align}</math>

Solving these equations gives

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat{a} &= m_1 - \sqrt{3 \left(m_2 - m_1^2\right)} \\
\hat{b} &= m_1 + \sqrt{3 \left(m_2 - m_1^2\right)}
\end{align}</math>

Given a set of samples <math>\{w_i\}</math> we can use the sample moments <math>\hat{m}_1</math> and <math>\hat{m}_2</math> in these formulae in order to estimate <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>.

Note, however, that this method can produce inconsistent results in some cases. For example, the set of samples <math>\{0,0,0,0,1\}</math> results in the estimate <math display="inline">\hat{a} = \frac{1}{5} \left(1 - 2 \sqrt{3}\right)=-0.4928</math>, <math display="inline">\hat{b} = \frac{1}{5} \left(1 + 2 \sqrt{3}\right)=0.8928</math>. Since <math>\hat{b}<1</math> it is impossible for the set <math>\{0,0,0,0,1\}</math> to have been drawn from <math>U(\hat{a},\hat{b})</math> in this case.

=== Binomial distribution ===
Let <math>W\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)</math> be [[Binomial distribution|binomially distributed]] with unknown parameters <math>n\in\N</math> and <math>p\in(0,1)</math>. The first two moments read as<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Shao |first=Jun |title=Mathematical Statistics |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-387-95382-3 |edition=2nd |pages=209}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&m_1=\operatorname E[W]=np, \\
&m_2=\operatorname E[W^2]=np(1-p)+n^2p^2.
\end{align}</math>

Solving these equations for the parameters yields<math display="block">\begin{align}
&p=\frac{m_1+m_1^2-m_2}{m_1}=1+m_1-\frac{m_2}{m_1}, \\
&n= \frac{m_1}{p}=\frac{m_1^2}{m_1+m_1^2-m_2}.
\end{align}</math>

Inserting the estimators <math>\hat m_1</math> and <math>\hat m_2</math> for <math>m_1</math> and <math>m_2</math> gives the corresponding moment estimators <math>\hat p</math> and <math>\hat n</math>.

This is a negative example, where the moment estimators have multiple issues: First, the estimator <math>\hat n</math> does not necessarily provide integers, although this can be easily resolved by rounding to the nearest integer.<ref name=":4" /> A more serious issue is that both estimators can lead to negative estimates, namely when <math>\hat m_1+\hat m_1^2-\hat m_2<0</math>, which is equivalent to the [[Variance|sample variance]] <math>S_n^2=\hat m_2-\hat m_1^2</math> being larger than the [[Sample mean and covariance|sample mean]] <math>\hat m_1</math>. This can happen, for example, in small data sets with large variation. In such cases, the moment estimators are useless.

=== Nonparametric estimation of mean and variance ===
The method of moment does not actually need any assumptions on the data distribution besides the existence of a certain number of moments. For the estimation of the mean <math>\mu</math> and the variance <math>\sigma^2</math> using observations <math>X_1,\dots,X_n</math>, assuming only <math>\operatorname E[X_i^2]<\infty</math>, the very same derivation as for the normal distribution (see above) applies, yielding the estimators

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat\mu &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \overline X, \\
\hat\sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(X_i-\overline{X}\big)^2.
\end{align}</math>

=== Estimation of polynomial probability densities ===
Another example application of the method of moments is to estimate polynomial probability density distributions. In this case, an approximating polynomial of order <math>N</math> is defined on an interval <math>[a,b]</math>. The method of moments then yields a system of equations, whose solution involves the inversion of a [[Hankel matrix]].<ref name="PolyD2">J. Munkhammar, L. Mattsson, J. Rydén (2017) "Polynomial probability distribution estimation using the method of moments". PLoS ONE 12(4): e0174573. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0174573</ref>
